subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story and Discussing Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read + Let us think — A. (pp.56–58): answer three questions about Meena, her anger, and her help

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story aloud from the textbook (pp.56–58), pausing at key moments — Meena launching boats, the boy overturning them, and the two making boats together — to invite brief observations from students.
Shared reading: teacher and students read the story together a second time, with students joining in on dialogue lines. Teacher draws attention to how Meena's mood shifts from anger to generosity.

Let us read + Let us think — A. ("answer questions about Meena, her anger, and her help"): teacher poses each question aloud, students respond orally in turn, then write their answers in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may answer question 3 vaguely — prompt them to describe the actual steps Meena showed (taking out coloured paper, demonstrating folding) rather than simply saying 'she helped him'. The story's resolution through generosity rather than continued anger is the heart of the narrative and worth underlining during shared reading.

periods.activity_title: True or False Check and Story Retelling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read + Let us think — C. (pp.58–59): judge four True/False statements about the story
Let us speak (p.60): tell the picture story of Manish saves the ant to the class

homework.task_brief: Let us think + Let us speak (p.59): discuss with a family member what else you can make with paper and what games you enjoy most

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads two sentences from the story aloud — the boy's remark that overturning boats is 'fun' and the moment Meena offers to help — to re-anchor students in the narrative before the True/False work.

Let us read + Let us think — C. ("True or False statements about the story"): teacher reads each statement aloud, students decide and write True or False, then the class discusses the correct verdict with a brief reason for each.
Teacher walks students through the six sequential pictures of Manish and the ant on p.60, eliciting what each picture shows before asking students to prepare their retelling.

Let us speak ("tell the Manish saves the ant picture story to the class"): pairs of students take turns retelling the picture story in their own words, with the teacher offering light guidance on sequence and connectives such as 'first', 'then', and 'finally'.

periods.teacher_notes: For the True/False task, students frequently confuse statement 2 — Meena ran home to complain — with what actually happened; guide them back to the story's text where Meena stays and confronts the boy directly. During the picture retelling, accept approximations of the plot and praise students who add detail about the ant's safety or Manish's care.

periods.activity_title: Pronouns He and She, and Position Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.61): fill in blanks using 'he' or 'she' for four sentences
Let us learn (p.62): choose the correct position word (on/under/in) for five picture-based sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two example sentences from the story aloud — 'She bent a little and launched a paper boat' and 'He gave it to Meena' — and asks students who 'she' and 'he' refer to, building understanding that these pronouns replace a person's name.

Let us learn — A. ("fill in blanks using he or she"): teacher reads each sentence pair aloud, students identify the named person's gender and write the correct pronoun, then the class checks answers together.
Teacher directs students to the bedroom picture on p.62 and names the objects visible — bat, bag, ball, car, books — pointing out their positions to build familiarity before the writing task.
Let us learn — B. ("choose the correct position word for five picture-based sentences"): students study the picture and select on, under, or in for each sentence, then compare answers with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes apply 'she' to any person without checking the name — remind them to look at the name in the first sentence before choosing. For the position words, encourage students to point physically at the object in the picture rather than guessing from memory.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A. (p.64): write a few lines about the park picture using eight given clue words

time_bands.activity: Teacher directs students to the park picture on p.64 and conducts a picture walk — pointing to the slide, see-saw, swings, and the children playing — and reads the eight clue words aloud together with students.

Modelled writing: teacher writes one or two sentences on the board using two of the clue words ('Children are playing in the park. They enjoy the swings.') and thinks aloud about how to connect ideas in a short description.

Let us write — A. ("write a few lines about the park picture using the eight clue words"): students write their own lines independently, using the picture and clue words as support. Teacher circulates and offers brief verbal prompts where students are stuck.
Two or three volunteers share what they wrote. Teacher highlights one strong sentence from each and encourages the class to applaud each sharer.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may list the clue words one per sentence without connecting them — invite them to use the park picture to decide what is happening so their writing tells a small story rather than a list. Accepting invented details about the children keeps writing lively; accuracy to the picture is the main anchor.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p.63): follow six steps to draw a rangoli pattern on the dot grid
Let us explore — B. (p.65): solve the toys-and-games crossword puzzle

homework.task_brief: Let us explore — A. (p.66): talk to elders at home, find out games they played, and be ready to share one with friends

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the six-step rangoli diagram on p.63 and walks through each step slowly, naming what is added at each stage so students can see the pattern build before they begin drawing.

Let us do ("follow six steps to draw a rangoli pattern on the dot grid"): students work individually, following each step in the textbook diagram. Teacher circulates, gently correcting dot-grid alignment where needed.
Students hold up their rangoli drawings briefly; teacher acknowledges variety in colour choices and encourages students to admire each other's patterns.

Let us explore — B. ("solve the toys-and-games crossword"): teacher reads each clue aloud while students look at the grid on p.65 and fill in answers. Across and Down clues are worked through together as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: For the rangoli, students often rush through the dot grid without following the step sequence — remind them to complete one step fully before moving to the next. The crossword clues use descriptive language that echoes the chapter's theme of games and play; treat it as a vocabulary celebration rather than a test.

items.source_lo: Student recalls and interprets story events using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Meena, paper boats, the naughty boy's reason, Meena's generous offer to teach folding.
items.item_stem: Why did the boy keep overturning Meena's paper boats in the stream?

options.label: A
options.text: He did not like the colour of the boats.

options.label: C
options.text: He wanted to take the boats home.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this may have confused the boy's later desire to play with a wish to take Meena's boats.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has read the boy's action as personal spite rather than thoughtless mischief.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student may be guessing without connecting the boy's own words to his motive.

items.source_lo: Student recalls and interprets story events using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Meena, paper boats, the naughty boy's reason, Meena's generous offer to teach folding.
items.item_stem: After the boy admitted he did not know how to make paper boats, Meena could have walked away. Instead, what did she do, and what does that tell you about her?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Meena took out coloured paper and showed the boy how to fold it into a boat. This shows she was generous and willing to share her skill even though the boy had upset her.

items.source_lo: Student retells a picture-sequence story using a sequential visual narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six-picture sequence of Manish rescuing an ant using a paper boat as a raft.
items.item_stem: Look at the six pictures on Textbook page 60. Which picture shows Manish placing a paper boat in the stream for the ant? Choose the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.text: The fifth picture, where Manish retrieves the boat.

options.label: B
options.text: The first picture, where Manish is walking.

options.label: C
options.text: The sixth picture, where the ant is safely on land.

options.label: D
options.text: The third picture, where Manish places the paper boat as a raft.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may not have followed the picture sequence carefully before answering.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has identified a later action and may be confusing placing and retrieving.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has jumped to the story's end without tracing the sequence that led there.

items.source_lo: Student retells a picture-sequence story using a sequential visual narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six-picture sequence of Manish rescuing an ant using a paper boat as a raft.
items.item_stem: Look at the pictures on Textbook page 60 and retell the story of Manish and the ant to your teacher or a partner. Use the words 'first', 'then', and 'finally' in your retelling.

expected_elements: Mentions Manish spotting the ant in the stream.
Describes the paper boat used as a raft.
Uses at least one sequence word correctly.

items.source_lo: Student composes short descriptive sentences using a picture and word prompts as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Park scene with children on slide, see-saw, and swings; eight clue words provided.
items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 64. Which clue word from the list — park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, happy — matches the tallest piece of equipment in the picture?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have focused on the see-saw's prominence rather than its height relative to the slide.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may associate swings with height but has not distinguished the slide as the tallest structure.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have chosen the most general word without linking it to a specific piece of equipment.

items.source_context: Park scene with children on slide, see-saw, and swings; eight clue words provided.
items.item_stem: Look at the picture on Textbook page 64. Write two or three sentences describing what the children are doing in the park. Use at least three of these words: park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, happy.

expected_elements: Mentions at least one specific piece of equipment.
Uses three or more clue words correctly.
Forms complete sentences with a subject and verb.

items.item_stem: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sentence | Choose the correct word
Meena took out coloured paper. ________ began to fold it carefully. | (he / she)
The boy watched closely. ________ wanted to learn. | (he / she)

items.source_context: Pronouns 'he' and 'she' replacing names; position words on, under, in describing object locations.
items.item_stem: Read the two sentences below. Replace the underlined name in the second sentence with 'he' or 'she' and write the full sentence. Then write one new sentence of your own using a position word — on, under, or in.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any correct substitution, e.g. 'Priya loves to draw. She draws every day.' Accept any position sentence, e.g. 'The book is on the table.'
